# Gluon Radiation from an Expanding Hydrodynamic Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma

This study investigates the gluon radiation emitted by the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion within the framework of the quark-gluon plasma. The primary objective is to characterize this radiation through two fundamental quantities: the density of states and the energy spectrum.

To this end, we calculate the density of states of the gluon radiation produced by the color current associated with the skyrmion configuration. This quantity provides essential information about the distribution of available radiation modes and serves as a foundation for understanding the emission properties of the system. Building upon this analysis, we further determine the energy spectrum of the gluon radiation arising from the same color current, thereby quantifying how the emitted energy is distributed across the relevant frequency range.

The physical context for this investigation is the quark-gluon plasma, a deconfined state of matter in which quarks and gluons are no longer bound within hadrons. This environment provides the natural setting for studying the dynamics of color currents and their associated radiative processes, making it particularly relevant for understanding the behavior of skyrmion-like structures under extreme conditions.

The calculations presented in this work are carried out using a semiclassical method, which offers a tractable yet physically meaningful approach to describing the radiation emitted by the color current. This methodology allows us to capture the essential features of the gluon emission while maintaining analytical clarity.

Finally, the results obtained through our analysis are compared with those reported in the existing literature. This comparison serves both to validate our findings and to situate them within the broader context of related studies, highlighting points of agreement as well as any novel aspects that emerge from the present treatment.

# Gluon Radiation from an Expanding Hydrodynamic Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma

## Introduction

The study of gluon radiation in the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) provides essential insight into the dynamics of strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions, such as those produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Among the various theoretical constructs used to model color-charged configurations, the skyrmion offers a particularly rich framework, encoding topological structure and collective behavior within a hydrodynamic description. In this work, we investigate the gluon emission arising from the color current associated with an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion embedded in the plasma.

## Theoretical Framework

We model the skyrmion as a topologically nontrivial field configuration whose expansion within the plasma generates a time-dependent color current. This current serves as the source term for the emission of gluon radiation. To compute the radiative properties of the system, we employ a semiclassical method, treating the color current classically while accounting for the quantized nature of the emitted gluons.

Within this approach, the density of states characterizes the available phase space for gluon emission, while the energy spectrum quantifies the distribution of radiated energy across the frequency domain. Both quantities are derived directly from the color current of the expanding skyrmion, with the semiclassical approximation providing a tractable yet physically meaningful description of the emission process.

## Results

Our calculations yield explicit expressions for the density of states and the energy spectrum of gluon radiation emitted by the skyrmion's color current. The density of states reflects the geometric and dynamical constraints imposed by the expanding configuration, while the energy spectrum reveals the characteristic frequency dependence of the radiated gluons. Together, these results capture the essential features of gluon emission driven by skyrmion dynamics in the plasma medium.

## Comparison with Existing Literature

To validate our findings, we compare the resulting spectra against established values reported in the existing literature. This comparison serves two purposes: first, it confirms the consistency of our semiclassical treatment with known results; second, it establishes a benchmark against which future calculations of skyrmion-induced gluon radiation can be measured. The agreement between our spectra and prior work lends confidence to the semiclassical methodology and its applicability to color-charged hydrodynamic configurations.

## Conclusion

By calculating the density of states and energy spectrum for gluon radiation from an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion, and by benchmarking these results against the literature, we provide a coherent framework for understanding gluon emission from skyrmion dynamics in the quark-gluon plasma. This work contributes to the broader effort to characterize color radiation processes in hot, dense QCD matter and offers a foundation for further studies of topological configurations in the plasma environment.

# The Results

Results are the outcomes that emerge from our efforts, decisions, and actions. Whether in science, business, education, or personal life, results serve as the tangible evidence of what we have accomplished—or failed to accomplish. They provide a measure against which we can evaluate our progress and refine our future approaches.

## Why Results Matter

The importance of results lies in their ability to transform abstract intentions into concrete reality. A plan, no matter how well-conceived, remains theoretical until it produces measurable outcomes. Results give us feedback, allowing us to understand whether our strategies work and where adjustments are needed.

In scientific research, the results section of a study is often the most critical component. It presents the data collected during experimentation, offering objective findings that either support or challenge the original hypothesis. These results must be reported honestly and clearly, as they form the foundation for conclusions and future research.

## Interpreting Results Correctly

Not all results are straightforward. Sometimes the outcomes we achieve differ from what we expected, and these surprises can be just as valuable as anticipated successes. A failed experiment, for instance, still teaches us something important about the boundaries of what is possible.

It is essential to interpret results within their proper context. A single result rarely tells the whole story. Factors such as sample size, external influences, and the methods used all shape how we should understand what we observe. Rushing to conclusions based on incomplete or misleading results can lead to poor decisions.

## Learning From Outcomes

Perhaps the greatest value of results is the opportunity they provide for growth. By analyzing what we have achieved, we gain insights that guide our next steps. Positive results reinforce effective habits, while disappointing results highlight areas for improvement.

Ultimately, results are not merely endpoints but stepping stones. They connect our past actions to our future possibilities, helping us build knowledge, capability, and wisdom over time.

## Conclusion

The results we produce reflect the quality of our thinking, planning, and execution. By treating results with honesty, careful analysis, and openness to learning, we can turn every outcome—whether success or setback—into a valuable source of progress.

**Gluon Radiation from an Expanding Skyrmion in a Quark–Gluon Plasma**

We investigate the emission of soft and semi-hard gluons associated with the dynamical expansion of a skyrmion embedded in a deconfined quark–gluon plasma (QGP). Modeling the baryonic soliton within an effective chiral Lagrangian coupled to the color field, we treat the time-dependent Skyrme profile as a classical source whose topological winding drives a radially expanding configuration during the pre-hadronization stage of a heavy-ion collision. By linearizing the Yang–Mills equations about the color-neutral background, we derive the induced gluon current and compute the differential radiation spectrum as a function of the soliton's expansion rate, size, and coupling to the surrounding medium. The medium is incorporated through a hard-thermal-loop resummed gluon propagator, allowing us to account for Debye screening and Landau damping in the plasma. We find that the accelerating boundary of the skyrmion produces a characteristic bremsstrahlung-like spectrum with an infrared enhancement regulated by the thermal screening mass, and that the total radiated energy scales quadratically with the expansion velocity in the non-relativistic regime while saturating for ultra-relativistic expansion. The angular distribution exhibits a dipole pattern whose orientation reflects the deformation of the topological charge density. We further estimate the back-reaction of gluon emission on the soliton dynamics, showing that radiative damping shortens the effective expansion lifetime by a factor sensitive to the plasma temperature. These results provide a semi-classical framework for connecting topological baryon dynamics to observable gluon emission and may offer insight into baryon stopping, energy loss, and entropy production in the early stages of relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

# Abstract

We present a semiclassical framework for computing gluon radiation from color currents propagating through the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Treating the fast partons as classical color charges coupled to the soft gluon field, we derive the medium-induced radiation spectrum accounting for multiple scattering and interference effects characteristic of the Landau-Pomeranchuk-Migdal (LPM) regime. The color current is described by Wong's equations, with the non-Abelian dynamics encoded in the precession of the charge in color space, while the emitted radiation is obtained from the classical Yang-Mills equations sourced by the current. We evaluate the resulting energy loss and its dependence on the medium properties, including the transport coefficient $\hat{q}$ and the path length through the plasma. Our results reproduce known limits in the coherent and incoherent regimes and provide a transparent physical picture connecting classical color dynamics to medium-induced parton energy loss. These findings have direct implications for the interpretation of jet quenching observables in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

# Abstract

We present a theoretical investigation of the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation emitted by high-energy partons traversing a quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Employing a semiclassical framework, we treat the fast projectile parton as a classical color source while describing soft gluon emission through the associated radiation field, allowing us to systematically capture medium-induced modifications to the vacuum bremsstrahlung spectrum. The interaction with the deconfined medium is modeled via multiple soft scattering, characterized by the jet quenching parameter $\hat{q}$, which encodes the transverse momentum broadening accumulated along the parton trajectory.

Within this approach, we derive analytic expressions for the gluon density of states and evaluate the differential energy spectrum $\omega \, dI/d\omega$ as a function of the emitted gluon energy and the medium length. Our results reproduce the characteristic Landau-Pomeranchuk-Migdal (LPM) suppression at intermediate energies, arising from the destructive interference of amplitudes over the coherence length, and exhibit the expected transition to the Bethe-Heitler regime for soft gluons. We further examine the dependence of the radiated energy loss on medium properties such as temperature and density, connecting the semiclassical parameters to thermodynamic quantities of the QGP.

The semiclassical treatment provides a transparent physical picture of the interplay between coherence, formation time, and multiple scattering, and offers a computationally tractable complement to fully quantum-mechanical formulations. These findings have direct relevance for the phenomenology of jet quenching observed in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions and may inform future extractions of transport coefficients from experimental data.

*Keywords:* quark-gluon plasma, gluon radiation, density of states, semiclassical approximation, LPM effect, jet quenching, parton energy loss
